title: Relations, ER models, keys, constraints and types
goal: Turn a business rule into keys and participation constraints, then test updates against them.
story:
Begin with the objects and their rules

Suppose a college stores students and courses. A student can take many courses, and a course can have many students. Names are not reliable identities: two students may share a name. Give each student a StudentID and each course a CourseID. The relationship Enrolment records a pair of identities. If the model permits at most one enrolment per student/course pair, that pair is its key. If repeated enrolment events are allowed, an event identifier or another distinguishing attribute is needed. The story determines the key.

A relation’s schema names its attributes and domains. Its current instance is the set of rows currently stored. A superkey determines a row uniquely in every permitted instance; a candidate key is a minimal superkey. The chosen primary key is one candidate, not a claim that no others exist. A current sample with distinct names does not prove a name is a key. A declared rule must justify that conclusion.

Separate cardinality from participation

“Each order has one customer” supplies a many-orders-to-one-customer relationship. It does not mean every customer has an order. Total participation requires every entity of the relevant type to take part; it is a separate minimum requirement. For a many-to-many relationship, store a relationship table with foreign keys to the two entity tables. A multivalued attribute such as a person’s phone numbers normally needs its own table rather than a repeating cell.

A foreign key requires a child value to match a referenced parent key, subject to null rules and the declared delete/update actions. In today’s exercises, child foreign keys are NOT NULL and parent deletion uses RESTRICT: you cannot remove a referenced parent until the references are dealt with. Inserting a valid new parent cannot itself make an existing child reference point to a nonexistent parent. Deleting a child also cannot create that particular referential failure. Other constraints still need checking.

Choose types for meaning, not appearance

A phone number or postal code is usually an identifier, even when it contains digits. Numeric arithmetic can lose leading zeros. Fixed-precision DECIMAL is appropriate when exact decimal amounts matter; binary floating point need not represent values such as0.1 exactly. NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY and FOREIGN KEY express different rules. SQL UNIQUE handling of nulls can vary by system, so questions that require a unique non-null identifier should state both uniqueness and NOT NULL.

Classical relational algebra uses sets; SQL query results usually retain duplicates unless DISTINCT or a set operation removes them. We will keep that distinction explicit on Days2–3.
worked: Make the relationship visible
A person may join many clubs and may have many phone numbers. Each club has many people. Map to relations; membership has at most one row per person/club pair.

Use Person(PersonID,…), Club(ClubID,…), Membership(PersonID,ClubID,…) with composite key(PersonID,ClubID), and Phone(PersonID,PhoneNumber) with a suitable pair key. Four relations separate entities, the many-to-many relationship, and the multivalued attribute. Total participation, if required, is an additional rule; it does not eliminate these structures.
Check an update, not a slogan
Customer IDs are{1,2}. Order rows(OID,CID) are(10,1),(11,1). CID is NOT NULL, a foreign key with RESTRICT. Can Customer1 be deleted?

No: both orders still reference1. Customer2 can be deleted because no order references2, assuming no other constraints. Inserting Customer3 is safe with respect to this foreign key, while inserting Order(12,3) is unsafe until parent3 exists.

title: Relational algebra and tuple calculus
goal: Translate set and quantifier statements into a reproducible query result.
story:
Make every operator answer a small question

Selection keeps rows satisfying a predicate. Projection keeps named columns and, in classical relational algebra, removes duplicate tuples. A Cartesian product pairs every row from one relation with every row from another. A join is a product restricted by a matching condition. A natural join equates every shared attribute name, not only the column you happen to think of as the key. Rename columns when the intended matches differ.

Set union, intersection and difference require compatible relation schemas. Difference R−S means rows in R that are absent from S; reversing it changes the question. To check that all observed child IDs occur among parent IDs, form child IDs minus parent IDs and test emptiness. This is a statement about the current instance, not a proof that a declared constraint exists for every future instance.

“Some” and “every” are different query designs

Let Enrol(Student,Course) contain(Ada,DB),(Ada,AI),(Ben,DB),(Cy,AI), and let Required(Course) contain DB and AI. Asking for students with some required course gives all three students. Asking for every required course gives only Ada. For each candidate student, search for a required course they lack. Keep the student exactly when that search finds no counterexample.

In tuple-calculus notation, the every-course test has the form Student(s) AND NOT EXISTS c in Required for which no matching Enrol row exists. In logic, a universal statement can be rewritten as the absence of an existential counterexample. In algebra, one construction is to form all candidate student/course pairs, subtract actual qualifying pairs to expose missing pairs, project the failing students, then subtract those students from the candidate set.

Restrict candidate tuples to explicit database relations. This keeps the query finite and avoids asking for an unlimited complement over every possible string or number. A tuple-calculus comprehension returns qualifying output tuples; multiple witnesses for one output do not duplicate it under set semantics.

The empty-requirement case checks understanding

If Required is empty, every explicitly listed candidate student meets the every-required-course condition: there is no missing required course. This is vacuous truth. An existential “has some required course” query instead returns none. Always specify the candidate Student relation; otherwise the intended universe is ambiguous.
worked: Projection changes cardinality
R(A,B)={(1,x),(1,y),(2,y)}. Compare πA(R) with SELECT A FROM R.

Classical projection is the set{1,2}, size2. The ordinary SQL SELECT retains duplicate1 values and has3 rows; SELECT DISTINCT A corresponds to the set projection. The row counts differ because the semantics differ, not because one query is necessarily wrong.
Find missing pairs
Use Enrol and Required above. Explain an algebraic every-course query.

Candidate students are{Ada,Ben,Cy}. The student×required product has6 pairs. Missing pairs are(Ben,AI) and(Cy,DB). Their projected students are{Ben,Cy}; subtracting from candidates leaves{Ada}. This calculation makes the universal condition visible as absence of a missing pair.

title: SQL: joins, groups, NULL and correlated queries
goal: Compute query outputs from the actual rows while tracking duplicate and null behavior.
story:
Follow the rows through the query

For the queries here, think in this logical order: FROM/JOIN forms candidate rows, WHERE keeps rows whose condition is TRUE, GROUP BY forms groups, HAVING filters groups, SELECT builds output columns, then DISTINCT/ordering may apply. This is a reasoning model for results, not a claim that the engine must physically execute in that order.

Ordinary SELECT keeps duplicates. A join can multiply rows: if a customer has three matching orders, the customer appears in three joined rows. A left join also retains an unmatched left row, with nulls in the right columns. COUNT(*) counts every result row; COUNT(right_key) counts only non-null right keys. Their difference matters on those unmatched rows.

NULL is not a hidden ordinary value

NULL represents missing or unknown information. Ordinary comparisons to NULL yield UNKNOWN rather than TRUE or FALSE. WHERE and HAVING keep only TRUE. Use IS NULL to test nullness. COUNT(column), SUM and AVG ignore null inputs; COUNT(*) does not. AVG divides by the count of non-null inputs, not the number of stored rows. SUM or AVG over no non-null inputs is NULL, not automatically zero.

NOT IN is dangerous when its subquery can return NULL. If no equality matches but one comparison is unknown, the negated membership test is still not TRUE, and the row is filtered. A correlated NOT EXISTS query can express the intended anti-match more directly, but explicitly decide whether null keys should qualify before calling the two queries equivalent.

Groups and correlated subqueries are different levels

WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING tests an aggregate property of a group. A correlated subquery contains a reference to the outer row, so its relevant comparison set can change for each row. To evaluate it on paper, write the outer ID and the subquery result side by side. This prevents the mistake of computing one global average when the query asks for a department average.

Always state ties and comparison direction. “Above average,” “at least average,” and “strictly more rows above than below” can select different records. ORDER BY is needed when output order matters; without it, a correct result set does not imply a guaranteed presentation order.
worked: Count the right objects
Sale(ID,Dept,Amount) has(1,A,10),(2,A,20),(3,B,20),(4,B,NULL),(5,C,5). Compute COUNT(*), COUNT(Amount), SUM(Amount), AVG(Amount).
The counts are5 and4. SUM is55, and AVG is55/4=13.75. The missing amount contributes neither a numeric value nor an extra denominator term to AVG.

For those sales, select rows whose Amount exceeds the average Amount of their own department.

Department averages are A15,B20,C5. Only ID2 has amount strictly above its local average. The null amount at ID4 fails the comparison. ID3 equals, rather than exceeds, B’s average; a global average would answer another question.

title: Functional dependencies, keys and normalization
goal: Derive keys and assess normal forms from dependencies, then test what a decomposition preserves.
story:
A dependency is a rule across all permitted rows

X→Y means that whenever two rows agree on attributes X, they must also agree on Y. A single agreeing pair does not prove the rule; a disagreeing pair can refute it. To compute X’s closure, start with X and repeatedly add the right side of any dependency whose left side is already present. Stop when no attribute can be added. X is a superkey if the closure contains the whole schema; it is a candidate key if no proper subset is also a superkey.

An attribute absent from every dependency’s right side must be supplied in each key, unless the full theory includes additional dependencies not listed. This is a useful search reduction, not a replacement for checking closure and minimality. We use exactly the stated dependencies and their logical consequences, and assume atomic attributes unless a question says otherwise.

Normal forms ask different questions

1NF is the atomic-domain starting convention used here. 2NF excludes a non-prime attribute’s dependency on a proper subset of a candidate key. Prime means belonging to some candidate key, not necessarily to the chosen primary key. 3NF requires, for every nontrivial dependency X→A in the closure of the dependency set, either X is a superkey or A is prime. BCNF removes the prime-attribute exception: every nontrivial determinant must be a superkey. A relation can therefore be in3NF but not BCNF.

Losslessness and dependency preservation concern a decomposition, not just each component’s normal form. A lossless decomposition reconstructs every permitted original relation by joining its projections without spurious rows. For a binary decomposition R₁,R₂ under functional dependencies, losslessness holds when the intersection functionally determines R₁ or R₂. Dependency preservation means the projected component constraints together imply the original dependencies, so they can be enforced without recombining relations. Neither property automatically gives the other.

Know the boundary of the first pass

Independent multivalued facts can create redundancy even in BCNF. For a Person–Hobby–Language table, if hobbies and languages vary independently for each person, a multivalued dependency can require all hobby/language combinations. A4NF decomposition separates PersonHobby and PersonLanguage. Independence is a semantic assumption; a small sample alone cannot establish it. Higher join-dependency/5NF practice belongs to the later-week extension when the selected syllabus interpretation or observed needs require it. Today’s diagnostic concentrates on FD closure through BCNF and binary decomposition.
worked: Prove a candidate key is minimal
R(A,B,C,D), F={A→B,B→C}. Find the candidate keys.

D never appears on a right side, so any key must contain D. No dependency produces A, so A is also mandatory. (AD)+ adds B then C, giving all four attributes. Removing A or D loses a required attribute, so AD is the sole candidate key. A+ is ABC, not the whole schema.
3NF does not imply BCNF
R(A,B,C), F={AB→C,C→B}. Analyze keys and the dependency C→B.

AB and AC are candidate keys. Thus every attribute is prime. C alone determines BC, not A, so it is not a superkey. C→B satisfies the3NF prime-right-side exception but violates BCNF. Decomposing into CB and AC is lossless because the intersection C determines CB, but AB→C is not preserved by the component FDs.

title: Files, index choice and B+ tree calculations
goal: Translate a page layout into an inequality and choose an index from the query predicate.
story:
Count physical units, not just records

A file stores records in pages or blocks. If records cannot straddle pages and headers are ignored, one page holds floor(page_bytes/record_bytes) records. The number of pages is the ceiling of record_count divided by that capacity. Taking one ceiling of total bytes divided by page size can be wrong because it lets fractions of records share unused space across pages.

A heap file supports simple insertion but does not sort its records by the searched field. A sorted file makes range scans natural but updates need care. An index is a separate access structure: it can reduce the pages searched while still requiring data-page reads for the matching records. Do not equate an index lookup with fetching the complete result for free.

Write the node’s contents before dividing

A B+ tree internal node with p child pointers has p−1 separator keys. With page size B, pointer size P and key size K, and no header, its layout requires pP+(p−1)K≤B. Solve for the largest integer p. A leaf has a different layout involving key/data-pointer entries and usually a next-leaf pointer; use the leaf’s stated convention instead of reusing the internal formula.

Separators guide search; record pointers are stored at leaves in the usual B+ model used here. Leaves are linked to support range scans. After a leaf split, the first key of the new right leaf is copied to the parent as a separator while remaining in the leaf. Internal-node splitting uses a different promotion convention. State capacity, insertion policy and split rule before tracing an update.

Match the index to the predicate

Hash indexes suit equality lookup but do not in general provide ordered range scanning. Ordered B+ indexes support equality and ranges. A composite ordered index on(A,B) orders first by A, then B inside each A region. A condition on A, or on A with a B range, can use contiguous key regions. A B-only predicate does not generally become one selective contiguous range; it may require scanning or implementation-specific techniques.

A clustered layout can place neighboring matching records on fewer data pages than an unclustered layout. Count cached root pages, index pages and data pages using the assumptions supplied. Bitmap indexes can help low-cardinality analytical attributes, but their benefit depends on workload and update behavior; “one index is always best” is not a valid universal rule.
worked: Internal fanout is an inequality
An internal page has1000 bytes, 8-byte child pointers, 8-byte keys and no header. Find maximum p.
The layout is8p+8(p−1)≤1000, or16p≤1008. Thus p≤63 and the maximum is63 pointers, with62 keys. Ignoring the extra pointer would change the answer.
Leaf split needs a convention
A leaf allows3 keys and currently has[5,9,13]. Insert11. Split four sorted entries evenly into two leaves, copy the right minimum upward.

title: Warehouses, OLAP, hierarchies and measures
goal: Define the fact grain, distinguish cuboids from result rows, and aggregate measures correctly.
story:
Declare what one fact row means

A fact table records measurements at a specified grain, such as one product sold at one store on one date. Dimension tables describe product, store and time. Changing the grain changes what can be added without double counting. A star schema connects dimensions directly to the fact; a snowflake design further normalizes dimension hierarchies. Neither name determines the correct grain for you.

A hierarchy orders detail levels, such as City→State→Country→ALL. Roll-up moves toward coarser groups; drill-down moves toward detail. Slicing fixes a dimension value, while dicing selects a subregion using conditions or sets. Pivoting changes the presentation orientation, not the underlying total. State the hierarchy instead of assuming that every attribute is naturally comparable.

Two different things are counted in cube questions

A cuboid is one selected aggregation level for each dimension. With d dimensions and only detail/ALL choices, there are2ᵈ cuboids. If dimension i has Lᵢ usable levels including ALL, and one level per independent hierarchy is chosen, the number of cuboids is the product of the Lᵢ. This is not the number of rows in a fully materialized cube.

For two dimensions with m and n distinct detail values, when every combination occurs and the only levels are detail and ALL, GROUP BY CUBE returns mn detail rows, m first-dimension subtotals, n second-dimension subtotals and one grand total. The row count is(m+1)(n+1). Missing combinations and filters can change row counts even though the cuboid types remain the same.

Not every measure can be added in every direction

Revenue and units sold are typically additive across independent dimensions. An inventory snapshot may be additive across stores but not across dates: adding today’s stock to yesterday’s stock does not give current stock. A rate or average cannot normally be summed. To combine averages correctly, keep sufficient statistics such as sum and count.

Distributive aggregates such as SUM and COUNT can be combined using the same fixed aggregate on partitions. Algebraic aggregates such as AVG can be reconstructed from a fixed collection like SUM and COUNT. An exact MEDIAN is holistic under the conventional classification: fixed-size partition summaries do not generally determine the exact combined median. These categories describe how much information aggregation must retain.
worked: Cube rows are not cube types
Product has2 values and Region has3, every combination occurs. Only detail and ALL levels are used. Count cuboids and GROUP BY CUBE rows.
There are2²=4 cuboids. Their row counts are6 detail rows,2 product subtotals,3 region subtotals and1 grand total:12 rows. The four aggregation types and twelve output rows answer different questions.
Keep sum and count
One group has10 records averaging20; another has30 averaging40. What is the combined average?
Recover totals:10×20=200 and30×40=1200. Combined average=(200+1200)/(10+30)=35. Taking(20+40)/2=30 would give the groups equal weight even though their record counts differ.

title: Preprocessing: normalization, discretization, sampling and compression
source: Han–Kamber–Pei3e Chapter3; DSC7e §4.5 types and§11.2 analytical context
goal: Choose a transformation from its goal, preserve its assumptions, and distinguish numerical scaling from schema normalization.
story:
Ask what information should survive

A transformation changes how data is represented. Scaling preserves numeric ordering under a positive affine map; discretization replaces detailed values with bins; sampling keeps a selected subset or draws; compression changes storage representation and may or may not preserve exact recoverability. These operations solve different problems. “Normalize” is overloaded: numeric normalization rescales values; relational normalization decomposes schemas using dependencies. Neither is a substitute for the other.

Scaling needs reference statistics

Min–max scaling to[0,1] uses z=(x−min)/(max−min), assuming max>min. Z-score standardization uses z=(x−mean)/standard_deviation, assuming a positive standard deviation. State whether supplied statistics are population or sample estimates if computing them; today’s questions supply the standard deviation directly. An input outside the reference min/max can transform outside[0,1]. That is not an arithmetic contradiction.

For prediction, fit scaling parameters using the training data, then reuse them on later data. Recomputing them using the test set changes the mapping and can leak information. If an attribute is constant, the standard formulas divide by zero; an explicit constant-feature policy is needed.

Bins and samples need boundaries and a model

Equal-width discretization divides a numeric interval into intervals of equal numeric length. Equal-frequency discretization aims for similar record counts, which need not produce equal widths; ties require a stated policy. Always specify which bin contains a boundary value. Replacing a number by its bin usually loses its exact original value.

Simple random sampling, stratified sampling and sampling with replacement use different probability models. Without replacement, a record can appear at most once in the selected sample. With replacement, repeated records are possible. Stratification samples within declared groups; it does not by itself make a combined unweighted estimate correct if sampling fractions differ. Preserve weights when the question requires a population estimate.

Compression requires a decoding story

Lossless compression permits exact reconstruction; lossy methods trade information for a reduced representation. Run-length encoding stores consecutive runs as(symbol,count), so it helps long runs and can expand alternating data. Dictionary and delta encodings exploit other patterns; a storage saving cannot be asserted without specifying the encoding sizes and overhead. A sample or a bin label is not generally an exact substitute for the full original data.

This final day also consolidates the full section: a well-normalized schema says little about whether a feature is standardized; a valid SQL result says little about whether its numerical average was reaggregated correctly. Translate the intended question first.
worked: Use the right statistics
An attribute has reference min10,max50,mean30,std10. Transform x=40 by min–max and z-score methods.

Min–max gives(40−10)/(50−10)=0.75. Z-score gives(40−30)/10=1. The outputs differ because the first measures position in a reference range and the second measures standard-deviation displacement from a mean.
Compression can expand
Encode AAABBCC using one byte per symbol and one byte per run count, ignoring headers. Compare ABAB.

AAABBCC has7 input bytes and3 runs, so encoding takes6 bytes. ABAB has4 bytes and4 runs, so its encoding takes8 bytes. The method is lossless in both cases; compressibility depends on the data pattern and the specified representation.
